summary: The article provides a generally reliable overview of ITR for freelancers, covering forms, methods, and deductions, with most claims verified against authoritative sources. However, some specific details regarding presumptive taxation limits and tax regime calculations need review.

claims.claim: Freelancers not requiring an audit must file their Income Tax Return (ITR) by August 31st for the previous financial year.
claims.note: For FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27), the ITR filing deadline for freelancers and professionals not requiring an audit (filing ITR-3 or ITR-4) is August 31, 2026.

claims.claim: ITR-3 is applicable to individuals and Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs) who have income from a "profession" and do not opt for the presumptive taxation scheme under Section 44ADA. This form is typically used by freelancers whose gross receipts exceed ₹50 lakhs in a financial year, or those who wish to declare a profit lower than 50% of their gross receipts (in which case an audit under Section 44AB becomes mandatory).
claims.note: ITR-3 is for individuals/HUFs with income from business or profession, including those with gross receipts exceeding ₹50 lakhs or those declaring lower profits requiring an audit. It is also used by freelancers who do not opt for presumptive taxation.

claims.claim: For freelancers and professionals, Section 44ADA is particularly relevant. This scheme allows professionals whose gross receipts do not exceed ₹50 lakhs in a financial year to declare 50% of their gross receipts as their taxable income.
claims.note: While the base limit for Section 44ADA is ₹50 lakhs, it has been increased to ₹75 lakhs if the cash receipts do not exceed 5% of the total gross receipts.

claims.claim: If your estimated tax liability for the financial year is ₹10,000 or more, you are required to pay advance tax in four instalments throughout the year. These instalments are due by June 15th (15% of total tax), September 15th (45% of total tax), December 15th (75% of total tax), and March 15th (100% of total tax).
claims.note: Freelancers with an estimated tax liability of ₹10,000 or more must pay advance tax in four installments: 15% by June 15, 45% by September 15, 75% by December 15, and 100% by March 15.

claims.claim: Section 80C: Investments in PPF, ELSS mutual funds, life insurance premiums, home loan principal repayment, NPS contributions (up to ₹1.5 lakhs).
claims.note: Section 80C allows a maximum deduction of ₹1.5 lakhs for various investments and expenses, including PPF, ELSS, life insurance premiums, home loan principal, and NPS contributions.

claims.claim: Section 80D: Health insurance premiums for self, family, and parents.
claims.note: Section 80D allows deductions for health insurance premiums paid for self, spouse, dependent children, and parents. The deduction limits vary based on age.

claims.claim: If you receive payments from foreign clients, this income is taxable in India, provided you are a Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) as per income tax rules.
claims.note: A Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) individual is taxable on their worldwide income, including foreign income.

The new tax regime slab rates for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27) are different. The slabs are: Up to ₹4 lakh (Nil), ₹4 lakh - ₹8 lakh (5%), ₹8 lakh - ₹12 lakh (10%), ₹12 lakh - ₹16 lakh (15%), ₹16 lakh - ₹20 lakh (20%), ₹20 lakh - ₹24 lakh (25%), Above ₹24 lakh (30%). Also, a rebate of ₹60,000 is available for income up to ₹12 lakh, making income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free.

article_title: ITR for Freelancers: Forms, Methods, and Deductions Explained
